claims.text: Annealing the 80%-cold-rolled Nb35Zr26Ti19Hf15Mo5 alloy at 750 °C for 20 minutes will induce partial recrystallization.
Annealing the 80%-cold-rolled alloy at 750 °C for 20 minutes will induce recovery.
The annealed microstructure will retain most of the cold-rolling-induced work hardening.
The formation of strain-free grains will enhance ductility.
The as-cast Nb35Zr26Ti19Hf15Mo5 alloy forms a single-phase BCC solid solution.
The as-cast alloy has approximately 100 μm equiaxed grains.
The as-cast alloy has a weak dendritic/interdendritic elemental distribution.
Annealing reduces dislocation density.
Annealing reduces the population of low- and medium-angle boundaries while preserving elongated grains and residual dislocation tangles.
Cold rolling introduces a high dislocation density and crystallographic texture.
The dislocation density and texture produced by cold rolling increase strength at the expense of ductility.
Annealing at 750 °C enables limited atomic diffusion that drives partial recovery and nucleation of recrystallized grains.
Recovery and recrystallized grains facilitate slip and reduce brittleness.
Residual dislocation blocking after annealing maintains most of the cold-rolling-induced strengthening.
The unannealed 80%-rolled alloy has approximately 1408 MPa tensile strength and 10.5% elongation.
The as-cast alloy has approximately 1007 MPa tensile strength and 23% elongation.
The 750 °C annealed alloy will have a modestly lower tensile strength than the unannealed 80%-rolled alloy.
The 750 °C annealed alloy will have significantly greater ductility than the unannealed 80%-rolled alloy.
Annealing at 750 °C for 20 minutes will improve the overall strength–plasticity balance relative to the unannealed 80%-rolled alloy.
Small changes in annealing temperature or duration may alter the balance between strength retention and ductility recovery.
